description: Team Relica is five teammates from Madinah, Saudi Arabia, with backgrounds in Information Technology, Data Science and Mechanical Engineering. We built RELICA: Still Here, a browser 3D story game where players become the machines NASA left on the Moon and Mars, carry out their real missions, then see the original NASA photos. Our skills: storytelling, creative direction, game engine and physics, world and character design, UX and sound. Play it: https://relica-pi.vercel.app
summary: RELICA: Still Here is a browser-based 3D story game in Arabic and English about the machines NASA left behind on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Instead of reading about them, players become them: they drive the Apollo 17 Lunar Roving Vehicle and repair its fender, gather evidence of ancient water with Opportunity, report hazards and fly with Ingenuity, recall Viking 1's first successful U.S. Mars landing, and point Pioneer 10's camera at Jupiter. After each task the original NASA photograph is revealed, so players see the real record behind what they just did. The game runs in any browser with no installation, which makes it easy to use in a classroom: a teacher can play one chapter and ask what the machine measured and why it mattered. Mission facts, dates and photographs come from NASA sources; the machines' voices and conversations are imagined to help young players care about real science.
details:
What it is

RELICA: Still Here is a short 3D story game that runs in any web browser, in English and Arabic. It follows five NASA machines that are still out there: the Apollo 17 Lunar Roving Vehicle (Moon, 1972), Viking 1 (Mars, 1976-1982), Opportunity (Mars, 2004-2018), the Ingenuity helicopter (Mars, 2021-2024) and Pioneer 10 (deep space, 1972-2003).

How it works

Each chapter turns the machine's real job into a mission the player performs: carry the crew and repair the rover's fender, examine three clues to ancient water on Mars (hematite spheres, jarosite and cross-bedding), scout hazards so the rover changes its route, frame a historical photo, and turn toward Earth to send it home. When a photo task is finished, the scene fades into the original NASA image with its date and credit, so players see the real record behind what they just did. A final memory wall shows each machine's planned and actual service; for example, Ingenuity was planned for 5 flights and flew 72.

NASA data in the game

- NASA 3D Resources models for the machines.

- Original NASA photos from the NASA Image and Video Library and Photojournal, revealed after photo tasks and on the memory wall, each with its NASA ID and credit.

- Mission records (dates, service, discoveries) from NASA Science mission pages and the Apollo Lunar Surface Journal.

- Moon and Mars gravity from the NASA Planetary Fact Sheets drives the physics, so players feel the difference while driving.

Benefits and intended impact

Students usually hear only about active missions. Relica lets school-age space fans and casual players learn by doing instead of reading: every key science fact is something they play. It builds an emotional connection with forgotten machines and an understanding of what they discovered. Teachers can use a single chapter in one lesson and ask what the machine measured and why it mattered. It is bilingual (English and Arabic), so it also reaches Arabic-speaking students.

Creativity

The machines are characters with their own voices and personalities, and each one's mission becomes a playable task. The "play the task, then see the real NASA photo" moment connects the story directly to the historical record.

Accuracy and factors we considered

Facts and photos are real and each one links to its NASA source in the repository. Faces, voices, conversations between machines and simplified routes are clearly dramatized. We chose careful wording: for example, Opportunity found evidence of past water (not liquid water today), and Viking 1 is described as the first successful U.S. Mars landing. We also designed for accessibility: no installation, modest hardware, English and Arabic, and clear on-screen key prompts.

Tools and technologies

JavaScript (ES modules, no build step), Three.js for 3D, Rapier for physics, HTML and CSS, the Web Audio API (all sounds and voices are generated in code), a small Python server for local runs, and Vercel for hosting. All assets are preloaded into memory with a real progress bar.
